claim: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) and atherosclerotic heart disease are frequently associated with dyslipidemia and hypertension.
source: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) and atherosclerotic heart disease, frequently associated with dyslipidemia and hypertension, represent significant health concerns.
evidence: This is a statement of established clinical knowledge about the comorbidities of CKD and atherosclerotic heart disease.

claim: oxLDL alone did not activate Gq signaling in CHO-LOX-1-AT1 cells.
source: Based on CHO and renal cell model experiments, oxLDL alone did not activate Gq signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from CHO cell model experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: When combined with Ang II, oxLDL significantly potentiated Gq-mediated inositol phosphate 1 production in cells expressing both LOX-1 and AT1.
source: However, when combined with Ang II, it significantly potentiated Gq-mediated inositol phosphate 1 production and calcium influx in cells expressing both LOX-1 and AT1 but not in AT1-expressing cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from cell-based assays measuring IP1 production.

claim: The potentiating effect of oxLDL on Ang II-induced Gq signaling was not observed in cells expressing AT1 alone.
source: However, when combined with Ang II, it significantly potentiated Gq-mediated inositol phosphate 1 production and calcium influx in cells expressing both LOX-1 and AT1 but not in AT1-expressing cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing CHO-LOX-1-AT1 cells with CHO-AT1 cells.

claim: The oxLDL-Ang II combination induces a unique receptor conformational change in AT1.
source: Conformational studies using AT1 biosensors have indicated a unique receptor conformational change due to the oxLDL-Ang II combination.
evidence: This is supported by data from AT1 biosensor experiments using FlAsH-BRET technology.

claim: Wild-type mice fed a high-fat diet with Ang II infusion presented exacerbated renal dysfunction.
source: In vivo, wild-type mice fed a high-fat diet with Ang II infusion presented exacerbated renal dysfunction, whereas LOX-1 knockout mice did not, underscoring the pathophysiological relevance of the AT1-LOX1 interaction in renal damage.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo experimental data from mouse models.

claim: LOX-1 knockout mice did not show exacerbated renal dysfunction when fed a high-fat diet with Ang II infusion.
source: In vivo, wild-type mice fed a high-fat diet with Ang II infusion presented exacerbated renal dysfunction, whereas LOX-1 knockout mice did not, underscoring the pathophysiological relevance of the AT1-LOX1 interaction in renal damage.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo experimental data comparing wild-type and LOX-1 knockout mice.

claim: The association between dyslipidemia and CKD involves a complex interplay of causality where CKD exacerbates dyslipidemia and dyslipidemia contributes to CKD progression.
source: It has been postulated that the association between dyslipidemia and CKD is not solely a result of epidemiological comorbidities but rather a complex interplay of causality, where CKD exacerbates dyslipidemia, while dyslipidemia, in turn, contributes to the onset and progression of CKD (Harper and Jacobson, 2008; Cases and Coll, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research literature.

claim: Moorhead et al. proposed the lipid nephrotoxicity hypothesis in 1982.
source: Since Moorhead et al. proposed the lipid nephrotoxicity hypothesis in 1982 (Moorhead et al., 1982), accumulating evidence has suggested that increased plasma lipid levels contribute to the development of renal glomerular and tubular damage, primarily in animal models of dyslipidemia (Ruan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citation to the original work.

claim: Increased plasma lipid levels contribute to the development of renal glomerular and tubular damage in animal models of dyslipidemia.
source: Since Moorhead et al. proposed the lipid nephrotoxicity hypothesis in 1982 (Moorhead et al., 1982), accumulating evidence has suggested that increased plasma lipid levels contribute to the development of renal glomerular and tubular damage, primarily in animal models of dyslipidemia (Ruan et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: LOX-1 expression is increased in hypertensive glomerulosclerosis.
source: The lectin-like oxLDL receptor, LOX-1, is implicated in organ damage caused by dyslipidemia, and its expression is increased in hypertensive glomerulosclerosis (Nagase et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: LOX-1 deficiency leads to a reduction in renal dysfunction precipitated by systemic inflammatory state following myocardial ischemia and injury in murine models.
source: In murine models, a deficiency of LOX-1 leads to a reduction in renal dysfunction, which was precipitated by a systemic inflammatory state following significant myocardial ischemia and injury (Lu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Hypertension and dyslipidemia act synergistically to induce renal dysfunction.
source: Hypertension is an established risk factor for CKD, and it has been suggested that hypertension and dyslipidemia act synergistically to induce renal dysfunction (Mänttäri et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: LOX-1 and AT1 are coupled on the plasma membrane.
source: We have shown that LOX-1 and the Ang II type 1 receptor (AT1) of the G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) are coupled on the plasma membrane, and that G protein-dependent and β-arrestin-dependent AT1 activation mechanisms are involved in the signaling mechanism by oxLDL and the intracellular uptake of oxLDL, respectively (Yamamoto et al., 2015; Takahashi et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous work.

claim: AT1 exhibits different modes and degrees of G protein activation depending on conformational changes induced by various ligands.
source: Interestingly, it was recently demonstrated that AT1 exhibits different modes and degrees of G protein activation depending on the conformational changes that occur during activation by various ligands (Wingler et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Gq-biased agonists induce a more open conformation of AT1 than Ang II, resulting in more potent activation of Gq.
source: Specifically, G protein αq subunit (Gq)-biased agonists induce a more open conformation of AT1 than Ang II, resulting in a more potent activation of Gq, which is the primary mediator of Ang II-induced hypertension.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Wingler et al., 2019).

claim: β-arrestin-biased agonists induce a closer conformational change in AT1, leading to β-arrestin activation without Gq activation.
source: In contrast, β-arrestin-biased agonists induce a closer conformational change, leading to the activation of β-arrestin without the activation of Gq (Wingler et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: oxLDL selectively activates Gi of AT1 without activating Gq.
source: Indeed, we found that oxLDL selectively activates G protein αi subunit (Gi) of AT1, without activating Gq (Takahashi et al., 2021), similar to that induced by β-arrestin-biased agonists (Namkung et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research including the authors' own work.

claim: The combination treatment of oxLDL and Ang II enhanced pro-inflammatory NFκB activity compared to each treatment alone in cells overexpressing both AT1 and LOX-1.
source: Indeed, we found that the combination treatment of oxLDL and Ang II enhanced pro-inflammatory NFκB activity compared to each treatment alone in cells overexpressing both AT1 and LOX-1 (Takahashi et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: oxLDL at concentrations of 10 and 20 μg/mL caused a leftward shift in the dose-response curve of Ang II for IP1 production, resulting in more than 80% decrease in EC50.
source: However, when oxLDL was supplemented at concentrations of 10 and 20 μg/mL (but not at 5 μg/mL), it caused a similar leftward shift in the dose-response curve of Ang II, resulting in a more than 80% decrease in the Effective Concentration 50 (EC50) (EC50 values: 0 μg/mL, 9.40×10⁻⁹ M; 5 μg/mL, 5.21×10⁻⁹ M; 10 μg/mL, 1.68×10⁻⁹ M; 20 μg/mL, 1.55×10⁻⁹ M).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing EC50 values at different oxLDL concentrations.

claim: The maximum IP1 production induced by Ang II in CHO-LOX-1-AT1 cells was unaffected by the addition of oxLDL.
source: The maximum IP1 production induced by Ang II in CHO-LOX-1-AT1 cells was unaffected by the addition of oxLDL.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from IP1 assays.

claim: oxLDL administration decreased Ang II-induced IP1 production in CHO cells expressing AT1 alone.
source: Additionally, we observed that oxLDL administration decreased Ang II-induced IP1 production in CHO cells expressing AT1 alone (CHO-AT1), in contrast to CHO cells expressing both AT1 and LOX-1 (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The potentiating effect of oxLDL on Ang II-AT1-Gq activity is dependent on the presence of LOX-1.
source: This finding suggests that the potentiating effect of oxLDL on Ang II-AT1-Gq activity is dependent on the presence of LOX-1.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data comparing cells with and without LOX-1.

claim: Native LDL did not alter Ang II-induced Gq activity in CHO-LOX-1-AT1 cells.
source: Native LDL, which does not bind to LOX-1, did not alter Ang II-induced Gq activity in CHO-LOX-1-AT1 cells (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Advanced glycation end products (AGEs) that bind to LOX-1 did not enhance Ang II-induced IP1 production.
source: Furthermore, the presence of advanced glycation end products (AGEs) that bind to LOX-1 (Jono et al., 2002), did not enhance Ang II-induced IP1 production (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d and citation to previous research about AGE binding to LOX-1.

claim: Enhanced IP1 production by co-treatment of oxLDL with Ang II was observed in CHO-cells expressing LOX-1 and mutated AT1 with impaired ability to activate β-arrestin.
source: We found that enhanced IP1 production by co-treatment of oxLDL with Ang II was similarly observed in CHO-cells expressing LOX-1 and mutated AT1 with impaired ability to activate β arrestin (Takahashi et al., 2021; Figure 1e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e and citation to previous work.

claim: The potentiating effect of oxLDL on IP1 production was unaffected by Pertussis Toxin (PTX), a Gi inhibitor.
source: Moreover, the potentiating effect of oxLDL on IP1 production was unaffected by Pertussis Toxin (PTX), a Gi inhibitor, or RKI-1448, a downstream Rho kinase inhibitor targeting G12/13 signaling in CHO-LOX-1-AT1 cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using pharmacological inhibitors.

claim: The potentiating effect of oxLDL on IP1 production was unaffected by RKI-1448, a downstream Rho kinase inhibitor targeting G12/13 signaling.
source: Moreover, the potentiating effect of oxLDL on IP1 production was unaffected by Pertussis Toxin (PTX), a Gi inhibitor, or RKI-1448, a downstream Rho kinase inhibitor targeting G12/13 signaling in CHO-LOX-1-AT1 cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using pharmacological inhibitors.

claim: The potentiating effect of oxLDL on IP1 production was completely inhibited by YM-254890, the Gq inhibitor.
source: However, this phenomenon was completely inhibited by YM-254890, the Gq inhibitor (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: The potentiating effect of oxLDL on Ang II-induced IP1 production is not influenced by β-arrestin, Gi, or G12/13.
source: These results suggest that the potentiating effect of oxLDL on Ang II-induced IP1 production is not influenced by β-arrestin, Gi, or G12/13, which are the main effectors of AT1 signaling aside from Gq (Lymperopoulos et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data with various inhibitors, supported by citation to previous research.

claim: oxLDL and low concentrations of Ang II (10–12 M) did not induce calcium influx in CHO-LOX-1-AT1 cells when treated alone.
source: We found that oxLDL and low concentrations of Ang II (10–12 M) did not induce calcium influx in CHO-LOX-1-AT1 cells when treated alone, but apparently, induced calcium influx when treated together (Figure 1g and h).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1g and 1h.

claim: oxLDL and low concentrations of Ang II (10–12 M) induced calcium influx in CHO-LOX-1-AT1 cells when treated together.
source: We found that oxLDL and low concentrations of Ang II (10–12 M) did not induce calcium influx in CHO-LOX-1-AT1 cells when treated alone, but apparently, induced calcium influx when treated together (Figure 1g and h).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1g and 1h.

claim: Ang II alone at higher concentrations (10–11 M) induced calcium influx, and no further enhancement was observed with oxLDL supplementation.
source: Ang II alone at higher concentrations (10–11 M) induced calcium influx, and no further enhancement was observed with oxLDL supplementation (Figure 1h).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1h.

claim: The combined effect of oxLDL and Ang II on calcium influx was completely blocked by YM254890.
source: The combined effect of oxLDL and Ang II on calcium influx was completely blocked by YM254890, suggesting that this phenomenon was Gq-dependent (Figure 1i).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1i.

claim: The combined effect of oxLDL and Ang II on calcium influx is Gq-dependent.
source: The combined effect of oxLDL and Ang II on calcium influx was completely blocked by YM254890, suggesting that this phenomenon was Gq-dependent (Figure 1i).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing blockade by Gq inhibitor.

claim: oxLDL supplementation with Ang II did not affect calcium influx in CHO cells expressing AT1 alone.
source: Importantly, oxLDL supplementation with Ang II did not affect the calcium influx in CHO cells expressing AT1 alone (Figure 1j).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1j.

claim: Treatment with Ang II resulted in a decrease in green puncta (AT1-eGFP) compared with the control group.
source: Our findings revealed a decrease in green puncta, which represent AT1-eGFP, upon treatment with Ang II, oxLDL alone, and their co-treatment compared with the control group (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Treatment with oxLDL alone resulted in a decrease in green puncta (AT1-eGFP) compared with the control group.
source: Our findings revealed a decrease in green puncta, which represent AT1-eGFP, upon treatment with Ang II, oxLDL alone, and their co-treatment compared with the control group (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Co-treatment with oxLDL and Ang II resulted in a decrease in green puncta (AT1-eGFP) compared with the control group.
source: Our findings revealed a decrease in green puncta, which represent AT1-eGFP, upon treatment with Ang II, oxLDL alone, and their co-treatment compared with the control group (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The extent of membrane AT1 reduction was similar across all treatment groups (Ang II, oxLDL, and co-treatment).
source: However, the extent of membrane AT1 reduction was similar across all the treatment groups (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: oxLDL treatment resulted in a reduction in red puncta representing LOX-1-mScarlet.
source: Consistent with our previous report (Takahashi et al., 2021), oxLDL treatment resulted in a reduction in the red puncta representing LOX-1-mScarlet (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a and citation to previous work.

claim: Co-treatment with oxLDL and Ang II did not further enhance the reduction of red puncta (LOX-1-mScarlet) compared to oxLDL treatment alone.
source: Importantly, co-treatment with oxLDL and Ang II did not further enhance the reduction of red puncta compared to oxLDL treatment alone (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Co-treatment with oxLDL and Ang II does not increase the content of activated AT1 compared to individual treatments alone.
source: Based on these findings, it is conceivable that co-treatment with oxLDL and Ang II does not increase the content of activated AT1 compared to individual treatments alone.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the receptor internalization data.

claim: In CHO-LOX-1 cells transduced with AT1-C-tailP1, 10–5 M Ang II and the combination of Ang II and 10 μg/mL oxLDL induced BRET similarly.
source: In CHO cells expressing LOX-1 alone (CHO-LOX-1) transduced with lentivirus encoding AT1-C-tailP1, 10–5 M Ang II and the combination of Ang II and 10 μg/mL oxLDL induced BRET similarly, whereas oxLDL alone did not alter BRET (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: oxLDL alone did not alter BRET in CHO-LOX-1 cells transduced with AT1-C-tailP1.
source: In CHO cells expressing LOX-1 alone (CHO-LOX-1) transduced with lentivirus encoding AT1-C-tailP1, 10–5 M Ang II and the combination of Ang II and 10 μg/mL oxLDL induced BRET similarly, whereas oxLDL alone did not alter BRET (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: In CHO-LOX-1 cells transduced with AT1-ICL3P3, the combination of Ang II and oxLDL induced BRET more prominently than Ang II alone.
source: In contrast, in CHO-LOX-1 cells transduced with AT1-ICL3P3-encoded lentivirus, the combination of Ang II and oxLDL induced BRET more prominently than Ang II alone, whereas oxLDL alone did not alter BRET (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: oxLDL alone did not alter BRET in CHO-LOX-1 cells transduced with AT1-ICL3P3.
source: In contrast, in CHO-LOX-1 cells transduced with AT1-ICL3P3-encoded lentivirus, the combination of Ang II and oxLDL induced BRET more prominently than Ang II alone, whereas oxLDL alone did not alter BRET (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The difference in BRET response between oxLDL and the combination treatment was abolished by a neutralizing antibody against LOX-1.
source: Furthermore, the difference between oxLDL and the combination treatment was abolished by a neutralizing antibody against LOX-1 (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: The concomitant binding of oxLDL to LOX-1 and Ang II to AT1 induces a conformational change in AT1 that is distinct from that induced by Ang II or oxLDL alone.
source: These findings suggested that the concomitant binding of oxLDL to LOX-1 and Ang II to AT1 induced a conformational change in AT1 that was distinct from that induced by Ang II or oxLDL alone.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the BRET biosensor data.

claim: oxLDL in combination with Ang II did not increase cellular IP1 content in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs).
source: We found that oxLDL in combination with Ang II did not increase the cellular IP1 content in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs), bovine vascular endothelial cells (BACEs), human aortic vascular smooth muscle cells (HAVSMCs), or rat macrophages (A10) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: oxLDL in combination with Ang II did not increase cellular IP1 content in bovine vascular endothelial cells (BACEs).
source: We found that oxLDL in combination with Ang II did not increase the cellular IP1 content in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs), bovine vascular endothelial cells (BACEs), human aortic vascular smooth muscle cells (HAVSMCs), or rat macrophages (A10) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: oxLDL in combination with Ang II did not increase cellular IP1 content in human aortic vascular smooth muscle cells (HAVSMCs).
source: We found that oxLDL in combination with Ang II did not increase the cellular IP1 content in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs), bovine vascular endothelial cells (BACEs), human aortic vascular smooth muscle cells (HAVSMCs), or rat macrophages (A10) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: oxLDL in combination with Ang II did not increase cellular IP1 content in rat macrophages (A10).
source: We found that oxLDL in combination with Ang II did not increase the cellular IP1 content in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs), bovine vascular endothelial cells (BACEs), human aortic vascular smooth muscle cells (HAVSMCs), or rat macrophages (A10) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In normal rat kidney epithelial cells (NRK52E), the combination of oxLDL and Ang II increased IP1 accumulation.
source: In contrast, in normal rat kidney epithelial cells (NRK52E) and fibroblasts (NRK49F), the combination of oxLDL and Ang II, but not Ang II alone, increased IP1 accumulation, which was suppressed in the presence of YM-25480, the Gq inhibitor (Figure 3a and b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3a and 3b.

claim: In normal rat kidney fibroblasts (NRK49F), the combination of oxLDL and Ang II increased IP1 accumulation.
source: In contrast, in normal rat kidney epithelial cells (NRK52E) and fibroblasts (NRK49F), the combination of oxLDL and Ang II, but not Ang II alone, increased IP1 accumulation, which was suppressed in the presence of YM-25480, the Gq inhibitor (Figure 3a and b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3a and 3b.

claim: Ang II alone did not increase IP1 accumulation in NRK52E and NRK49F cells.
source: In contrast, in normal rat kidney epithelial cells (NRK52E) and fibroblasts (NRK49F), the combination of oxLDL and Ang II, but not Ang II alone, increased IP1 accumulation, which was suppressed in the presence of YM-25480, the Gq inhibitor (Figure 3a and b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3a and 3b.

claim: IP1 accumulation induced by co-treatment with Ang II and oxLDL in NRK52E and NRK49F cells was suppressed by YM-25480, the Gq inhibitor.
source: In contrast, in normal rat kidney epithelial cells (NRK52E) and fibroblasts (NRK49F), the combination of oxLDL and Ang II, but not Ang II alone, increased IP1 accumulation, which was suppressed in the presence of YM-25480, the Gq inhibitor (Figure 3a and b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3a and 3b.

claim: IP1 accumulation induced by co-treatment with Ang II and oxLDL was abolished by siRNA-mediated knockdown of AT1 in NRK52E and NRK49F cells.
source: IP1 accumulation induced by co-treatment with Ang II and oxLDL was abolished by the siRNA-mediated knockdown of either AT1 or LOX-1 (Figure 3c and d; the knockdown efficacy is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3c and 3d.

claim: IP1 accumulation induced by co-treatment with Ang II and oxLDL was abolished by siRNA-mediated knockdown of LOX-1 in NRK52E and NRK49F cells.
source: IP1 accumulation induced by co-treatment with Ang II and oxLDL was abolished by the siRNA-mediated knockdown of either AT1 or LOX-1 (Figure 3c and d; the knockdown efficacy is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3c and 3d.

claim: Treatment with 10–7 M Ang II alone did not increase intracellular calcium concentrations in NRK49F cells.
source: Regarding calcium influx, intracellular calcium concentrations were not increased by the treatment of either 10–7 M Ang II or low concentration of oxLDL (2 μg/ml) alone (Figure 3e, left and middle, Figure 3f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3e and 3f.

claim: Treatment with low concentration of oxLDL (2 μg/ml) alone did not increase intracellular calcium concentrations in NRK49F cells.
source: Regarding calcium influx, intracellular calcium concentrations were not increased by the treatment of either 10–7 M Ang II or low concentration of oxLDL (2 μg/ml) alone (Figure 3e, left and middle, Figure 3f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3e and 3f.

claim: The combination of Ang II (10–7 M) and oxLDL (2 μg/ml) increased intracellular Ca2+ concentration in NRK49F cells.
source: In contrast, the combination of Ang II (10–7 M) and oxLDL (2 μg/ml) increased intracellular Ca2+ concentration (Figure 3e, right, Figure 3f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3e and 3f.

claim: The combined effect of oxLDL and Ang II on calcium influx in NRK49F cells was attenuated by siRNA knockdown of AT1.
source: The combined effect on calcium influx was attenuated by the siRNA knockdown of either AT1 or LOX-1 (Figure 3g).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3g.

claim: The combined effect of oxLDL and Ang II on calcium influx in NRK49F cells was attenuated by siRNA knockdown of LOX-1.
source: The combined effect on calcium influx was attenuated by the siRNA knockdown of either AT1 or LOX-1 (Figure 3g).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3g.

claim: The Gq inhibitor inhibited the combined effect of oxLDL and Ang II on calcium influx in NRK49F cells.
source: The Gq inhibitor and angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB), Irbesartan, also inhibited this phenomenon (Figure 3h).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3h.

claim: Irbesartan, an angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB), inhibited the combined effect of oxLDL and Ang II on calcium influx in NRK49F cells.
source: The Gq inhibitor and angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB), Irbesartan, also inhibited this phenomenon (Figure 3h).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3h.

claim: Calcium influx was not induced by either combination therapy or monotherapy in NRK52E cells.
source: Calcium influx was not induced by either combination therapy or monotherapy in NRK52E cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Co-treatment of oxLDL and Ang II increased mRNA levels of NADPH components Ncf2 and Cybb in NRK49F cells compared to vehicle.
source: In NRK49F cells, co-treatment of oxLDL and Ang II, compared to vehicle, increased mRNA levels of NADPH components, Ncf2 and Cybb, fibrosis markers, Fn1, Col1a1, Col4a1, and Tgfb2, and inflammatory cytokines, Tnf, Il1b, Il6, and Ccl2 (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Co-treatment of oxLDL and Ang II increased mRNA levels of fibrosis markers Fn1, Col1a1, Col4a1, and Tgfb2 in NRK49F cells compared to vehicle.
source: In NRK49F cells, co-treatment of oxLDL and Ang II, compared to vehicle, increased mRNA levels of NADPH components, Ncf2 and Cybb, fibrosis markers, Fn1, Col1a1, Col4a1, and Tgfb2, and inflammatory cytokines, Tnf, Il1b, Il6, and Ccl2 (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Co-treatment of oxLDL and Ang II increased mRNA levels of inflammatory cytokines Tnf, Il1b, Il6, and Ccl2 in NRK49F cells compared to vehicle.
source: In NRK49F cells, co-treatment of oxLDL and Ang II, compared to vehicle, increased mRNA levels of NADPH components, Ncf2 and Cybb, fibrosis markers, Fn1, Col1a1, Col4a1, and Tgfb2, and inflammatory cytokines, Tnf, Il1b, Il6, and Ccl2 (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: oxLDL did not alter the expression of genes of interest in NRK49F cells.
source: Notably, oxLDL did not alter the expression of the genes of interest, and Ang II increased the mRNA levels of only Fn1 and Ccl2, indicating the apparent synergistic effect of co-treatment with Ang II and oxLDL on specific gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from gene expression analysis.

claim: Ang II increased the mRNA levels of only Fn1 and Ccl2 in NRK49F cells.
source: Notably, oxLDL did not alter the expression of the genes of interest, and Ang II increased the mRNA levels of only Fn1 and Ccl2, indicating the apparent synergistic effect of co-treatment with Ang II and oxLDL on specific gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from gene expression analysis.

claim: Co-treatment with Ang II and oxLDL has a synergistic effect on specific gene expression in NRK49F cells.
source: Notably, oxLDL did not alter the expression of the genes of interest, and Ang II increased the mRNA levels of only Fn1 and Ccl2, indicating the apparent synergistic effect of co-treatment with Ang II and oxLDL on specific gene expression.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the gene expression data.

claim: The amplification effect of co-treatment with oxLDL and Ang II was observed in limited genes including Ncf2, Tgfb2, Il6, and Ccl2 in NRK52E cells.
source: This amplification effect of co-treatment was also observed in limited genes including Ncf2, Tgfb2, Il6, and Ccl2 in NRK52E cells (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The combined effects of oxLDL and Ang II on gene expression were completely abolished by the Gq inhibitor in NRK49F and NRK52E cells.
source: The combined effects of oxLDL and Ang II on gene expression were completely abolished by the Gq inhibitor (Figure 4c and d) and ARB (Figure 4e and f) in NRK49F and NRK 52E.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4c and 4d.

claim: The combined effects of oxLDL and Ang II on gene expression were completely abolished by ARB in NRK49F and NRK52E cells.
source: The combined effects of oxLDL and Ang II on gene expression were completely abolished by the Gq inhibitor (Figure 4c and d) and ARB (Figure 4e and f) in NRK49F and NRK 52E.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4e and 4f.

claim: The combination of Ang II (10–7 M) and oxLDL (5 μg/mL) induced αSMA expression in NRK49F cells to the same extent as TGFβ.
source: The combination of Ang II (10–7 M) and oxLDL (5 μg/mL) induced αSMA expression in NRK49F or NRK52E to the same extent or less than TGFβ, a major inducer of EMT, respectively (Figure 5a and b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5a and 5b.

claim: The combination of Ang II (10–7 M) and oxLDL (5 μg/mL) induced αSMA expression in NRK52E cells to a lesser extent than TGFβ.
source: The combination of Ang II (10–7 M) and oxLDL (5 μg/mL) induced αSMA expression in NRK49F or NRK52E to the same extent or less than TGFβ, a major inducer of EMT, respectively (Figure 5a and b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5a and 5b.

claim: oxLDL treatment alone did not affect αSMA expression in NRK49F and NRK52E cells.
source: The results of the combination treatment were strikingly different from that of oxLDL or Ang II treatment alone, which did not affect αSMA expression in both types of cells (Figure 5c and d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5c and 5d.

claim: Ang II treatment alone did not affect αSMA expression in NRK49F and NRK52E cells.
source: The results of the combination treatment were strikingly different from that of oxLDL or Ang II treatment alone, which did not affect αSMA expression in both types of cells (Figure 5c and d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5c and 5d.

claim: The induction of αSMA by the combined treatment of oxLDL and Ang II was suppressed in the presence of a Gq inhibitor in NRK49F and NRK52E cells.
source: The induction of αSMA by the combined treatment was suppressed in the presence of a Gq inhibitor or ARB in both types of cells, suggesting the AT1-Gq-dependent pathway in this phenomenon (Figure 5e, f, g and h).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5e, 5f, 5g, and 5h.

claim: The induction of αSMA by the combined treatment of oxLDL and Ang II was suppressed in the presence of ARB in NRK49F and NRK52E cells.
source: The induction of αSMA by the combined treatment was suppressed in the presence of a Gq inhibitor or ARB in both types of cells, suggesting the AT1-Gq-dependent pathway in this phenomenon (Figure 5e, f, g and h).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5e, 5f, 5g, and 5h.

claim: The induction of αSMA by combined treatment of oxLDL and Ang II occurs through an AT1-Gq-dependent pathway.
source: The induction of αSMA by the combined treatment was suppressed in the presence of a Gq inhibitor or ARB in both types of cells, suggesting the AT1-Gq-dependent pathway in this phenomenon (Figure 5e, f, g and h).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing suppression by Gq inhibitor and ARB.

claim: Ang II alone increased BrdU incorporation in NRK49F cells.
source: When administered alone, Ang II and oxLDL increased and reduced BrdU incorporation, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from BrdU assays.

claim: oxLDL alone reduced BrdU incorporation in NRK49F cells.
source: When administered alone, Ang II and oxLDL increased and reduced BrdU incorporation, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from BrdU assays.

claim: The reducing effect of oxLDL on proliferation was blocked by Irbesartan but not by a Gq inhibitor.
source: The reducing effect of oxLDL on proliferation was blocked by Irbesartan, but not by a Gq inhibitor, consistent with our findings that oxLDL induces biased activation of AT1, which favors Gi but not Gq signaling (Takahashi et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from BrdU assays and citation to previous work.

claim: oxLDL potentiated the Ang II-induced increase in BrdU incorporation in NRK49F cells.
source: Oxidized LDL potentiated the Ang II-induced increase in BrdU incorporation, which was blocked in the presence of a Gq inhibitor or an ARB (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: The potentiation of Ang II-induced BrdU incorporation by oxLDL was blocked by a Gq inhibitor.
source: Oxidized LDL potentiated the Ang II-induced increase in BrdU incorporation, which was blocked in the presence of a Gq inhibitor or an ARB (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: The potentiation of Ang II-induced BrdU incorporation by oxLDL was blocked by an ARB.
source: Oxidized LDL potentiated the Ang II-induced increase in BrdU incorporation, which was blocked in the presence of a Gq inhibitor or an ARB (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: siRNA-mediated knockdown of AT1 completely abolished the effects of Ang II and oxLDL, either alone or in combination, on BrdU incorporation in NRK49F cells.
source: The siRNA-mediated knockdown of AT1 completely abolished the effects of Ang II and oxLDL, either alone or in combination.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from BrdU assays with siRNA knockdown.

claim: Knockdown of LOX-1 did not affect the pro-proliferative effect of Ang II itself in NRK49F cells.
source: Knockdown of LOX-1 did not affect the pro-proliferative effect of Ang II itself but blocked the enhanced proliferation induced by co-treatment with oxLDL (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Knockdown of LOX-1 blocked the enhanced proliferation induced by co-treatment with oxLDL and Ang II in NRK49F cells.
source: Knockdown of LOX-1 did not affect the pro-proliferative effect of Ang II itself but blocked the enhanced proliferation induced by co-treatment with oxLDL (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: The high-fat diet (HFD) used in the study prominently increased the plasma LOX-1 ligand concentration in mice after 6 weeks of feeding.
source: Consistent with a previous report (Fujita et al., 2009), the HFD used in the study prominently increased the plasma LOX-1 ligand concentration, which was undetectable under a normal diet (ND) after 6 wk of feeding (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and citation to previous research.

claim: The HFD did not intensify but rather attenuated the body weight increase during the experimental period compared to the ND.
source: Notably, the HFD did not intensify but rather attenuated the body weight increase during the experimental period compared to the ND (Figure 7—figure supplement 2a–c), likely due to reduced food intake in mice fed the HFD used in this study (Figure 7—figure supplement 2d, e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The pressor dose of Ang II similarly increased BP in HFD-fed and ND-fed WT mice.
source: The pressor dose of Ang II similarly increased BP in HFD-fed and ND-fed WT mice (Figure 7b, Figure 7—figure supplement 2f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7b and Figure 7—figure supplement 2f.

claim: There was a modest trend of attenuated BP elevation by 0.7 γ Ang II infusion in LOX-1 KO mice.
source: However, notably, there was a modest trend of attenuated BP elevation by 0.7 γ Ang II infusion in LOX-1 KO mice, in line with the previous report showing reduced Ang II-induced BP elevation by LOX-1 deficiency in mice (Figure 7b, Figure 7—figure supplement 2f; Hu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7b and Figure 7—figure supplement 2f, and citation to previous research.

claim: A subpressor dose of Ang II did not alter BP in the corresponding mouse groups.
source: As expected, a subpressor dose of Ang II did not alter BP in the corresponding mouse group (Figure 7b, Figure 7—figure supplement 2g).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7b and Figure 7—figure supplement 2g.

claim: HFD with saline infusion did not alter the urinary 8-OHdG concentration in WT or LOX-1 KO mice compared to ND with saline infusion.
source: Regarding biofluid analysis, HFD with saline infusion did not alter the urinary 8-OHdG concentration as a marker of oxidative stress and urinary albumin excretion (UAE) compared to ND with saline infusion in either WT or LOX-1 KO mice (Figure 7c and d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7c and 7d.

claim: HFD with saline infusion did not alter urinary albumin excretion (UAE) in WT or LOX-1 KO mice compared to ND with saline infusion.
source: Regarding biofluid analysis, HFD with saline infusion did not alter the urinary 8-OHdG concentration as a marker of oxidative stress and urinary albumin excretion (UAE) compared to ND with saline infusion in either WT or LOX-1 KO mice (Figure 7c and d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7c and 7d.

claim: The pressor dose of Ang II with ND significantly increased the urinary 8-OHdG concentration in WT mice.
source: The pressor dose of Ang II with ND significantly increased the urinary 8-OHdG concentration and UAE in WT mice (Figure 7c and d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7c and 7d.

claim: The pressor dose of Ang II with ND significantly increased UAE in WT mice.
source: The pressor dose of Ang II with ND significantly increased the urinary 8-OHdG concentration and UAE in WT mice (Figure 7c and d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7c and 7d.

claim: HFD feeding in WT mice with a pressor dose of Ang II resulted in a prominent increase in urinary 8-OHdG concentration compared to mice fed with ND.
source: Notably, HFD feeding in WT mice with a pressor dose of Ang II resulted in a prominent increase in urinary 8-OHdG concentration and UAE compared to mice fed with ND (Figure 7c and d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7c and 7d.

claim: HFD feeding in WT mice with a pressor dose of Ang II resulted in a prominent increase in UAE compared to mice fed with ND.
source: Notably, HFD feeding in WT mice with a pressor dose of Ang II resulted in a prominent increase in urinary 8-OHdG concentration and UAE compared to mice fed with ND (Figure 7c and d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7c and 7d.

claim: In WT mice administered with a subpressor dose of Ang II, a significant increase in UAE was observed when comparing the effects of HFD to ND.
source: In WT mice administered with a subpressor dose of Ang II, a significant increase in UAE was observed when comparing the effects of HFD to ND (Figure 7d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7d.

claim: There were no significant differences in urinary 8-OHdG levels between HFD and ND in WT mice administered with a subpressor dose of Ang II.
source: There were no significant differences in urinary 8-OHdG levels between the two dietary conditions (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7c.

claim: When LOX-1 KO mice were fed either HFD or ND and then administered the corresponding dose of Ang II, no differences were observed in urinary 8-OHdG and UAE.
source: Interestingly, when LOX-1 KO mice were fed either HFD or ND and then administered the corresponding dose of Ang II, no differences were observed in the measured parameters (Figure 7c and d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7c and 7d.

claim: The combination of HFD and Ang II administration has a more pronounced effect on certain biofluid markers of renal injury in WT mice than in LOX-1 KO mice.
source: These findings indicate that the combination of HFD and Ang II administration appears to have a more pronounced effect on certain biofluid markers of renal injury in WT mice than in LOX-1 KO mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data comparing WT and LOX-1 KO mice.

claim: There was no difference in plasma aldosterone concentration between ND- and HFD-fed WT mice with a pressor dose of Ang II.
source: We did not find a difference in plasma aldosterone concentration between ND- and HFD-fed WT mice with a pressor dose of Ang II (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: In mice treated with a pressor dose of Ang II, 15 out of 18 genes examined showed enhanced alterations in gene expression indicative of heightened NADPH oxidase components, inflammatory cytokines, fibrosis, decreased epithelial markers, and exacerbated tubular injury in HFD-fed WT mice compared to ND-fed mice.
source: In mice treated with a pressor dose of Ang II, 15 out of 18 genes examined showed enhanced alterations in gene expression, indicative of heightened NADPH oxidase components, inflammatory cytokines, fibrosis, decreased epithelial markers, and exacerbated tubular injury in HFD-fed WT mice compared to ND-fed mice (Figure 8a, Figure 8—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8a and Figure 8—figure supplement 1a.

claim: For many genes, a synergistic effect of the combination of a pressor dose of Ang II and HFD was not observed in LOX-1 KO mice.
source: For many of these genes, a synergistic effect of the combination of a pressor dose of Ang II and HFD was not observed in LOX-1 KO mice (Figure 8a, Figure 8—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8a and Figure 8—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Seven genes displayed discernible differences between HFD- and ND-fed WT mice treated with a subpressor dose of Ang II.
source: Seven genes displayed discernible differences between HFD- and ND-fed WT mice treated with a subpressor dose of Ang II (Figure 8b, Figure 8—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8b and Figure 8—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Other than fibronectin, no differences were observed between ND- and HFD-fed LOX-1 mice exposed to a subpressor dose of Ang II.
source: Other than fibronectin, no differences were observed between ND- and HFD-fed LOX-1 mice exposed to a subpressor dose of Ang II (Figure 8b, Figure 8—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8b and Figure 8—figure supplement 1b.

claim: No variations emerged in Agtr1a and Olr1 expression between the ND and HFD groups when subjected to the corresponding dose of Ang II treatment in both WT and LOX-1 KO mice.
source: In relation to Agtr1a and Olr1 expression, no variations emerged between the ND and HFD groups when subjected to the corresponding dose of Ang II treatment in both WT and LOX-1 KO mice (Figure 8—figure supplement 1a, b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1a and 1b.

claim: The administration of either a subpressor or pressor dose of Ang II, both in isolation and in combination with HFD for 4 weeks, did not reveal any notable increase in fibrosis as evaluated by Masson-Trichrome staining.
source: In the histological analysis of kidney samples, in contrast to the gene expression data, the administration of either a subpressor or pressor dose of Ang II, both in isolation and in combination with HFD for 4 wk, did not reveal any notable increase in fibrosis, as evaluated by Masson-Trichrome staining (Figure 9—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1a.

claim: There was no significant change in the degree of mesangial expansion or glomerular area as assessed by PAS staining.
source: Similarly, there was no significant change in the degree of mesangial expansion or glomerular area, as assessed by PAS staining. (Figure 9—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1b.

claim: LOX-1 and AT1a were predominantly colocalized in the renal tubules, but not in the glomeruli.
source: As shown in Figure 9a and b, LOX-1 and AT1a were predominantly colocalized in the renal tubules, but not in the glomeruli.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figures 9a and 9b.

claim: Both AT1 and LOX-1 colocalize with megalin, especially at the brush borders, indicating their presence within the same renal compartments.
source: Both AT1 and LOX-1 were observed to colocalize with megalin, especially at the brush borders, indicating their presence within the same renal compartments involved in AT1/LOX-1 signaling.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2.

claim: The simultaneous binding of Ang II to AT1 and oxLDL to LOX-1 triggers distinct and more pronounced structural modifications in AT1 than the individual modifications induced by each ligand.
source: We propose that the simultaneous binding of Ang II to AT1 and oxLDL to LOX-1 triggers distinct and more pronounced structural modifications in AT1 than the individual modifications induced by each ligand.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: The structural alteration in AT1 caused by simultaneous binding of Ang II and oxLDL leads to the enhanced activation of Gq signaling.
source: This structural alteration in AT1 leads to the enhanced activation of Gq signaling.
evidence: This is a key conclusion of the study, supported by multiple experimental findings.

claim: The binding of both oxLDL and Ang II to LOX-1 and AT1, respectively, may result in a more open AT1 structure, leading to stronger downstream Gq signaling.
source: Based on our findings and the aforementioned structure-activity relationship of AT1, we hypothesized that the binding of both oxLDL and Ang II to LOX-1 and AT1, respectively, may result in a more open AT1 structure, leading to stronger downstream Gq signaling.
evidence: This is the central hypothesis of the study.
